opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about quite a lot, because looking back, my research career maps almost exactly onto these paradigm shifts.

When I started my PhD, computer vision was in what I'd call the hand-crafted era. We designed features by hand, thought carefully about optimization, and built graphical models. A lot of my early work was on things like segmentation and superpixels, where you set up an objective, maybe a submodular function or a graph-based formulation, and then find a clever way to optimize it. The mindset was: the researcher's insight lives in the model structure.

Then deep learning arrived, and the key ingredient shifted from hand-designed structure to data plus compute plus learnable architectures. Honestly, it was a bit humbling. Many problems we had worked on very carefully were suddenly solved better by a convolutional network trained on enough data. When I moved toward generative modeling, first with GANs, working on unsupervised image-to-image translation and then semantic image synthesis like GauGAN, the questions changed. It was less "how do I write down the right energy function" and more "how do I design the learning setup so the network discovers the structure itself."

Now we're in the era of foundation models and scaling, with diffusion models, transformers, and large-scale video and world models. The leverage is even more in data curation, infrastructure, and scale.

So how do I make sense of the earlier work? I don't think of it as wasted. Two things carry over. First, the problems themselves persist. We still care about structure, correspondence, consistency, and controllability. The old literature tells you what the hard parts are, even if the tools change. Second, the habit of thinking rigorously about what an objective really encourages is still very valuable. When you train a huge model, understanding what your loss and your data actually incentivize is essentially the same skill we used when designing energy functions.

But I also try not to hold on too tightly. The lesson I've taken from going through several paradigms is that the methods are temporary. What lasts is good taste in problems, and the willingness to let go of your own past techniques when something more general and scalable comes along. Each time I've done that, it felt uncomfortable at first, and each time it turned out to be the right move.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes shifts toward more scalable methods and says the methods are temporary, but does not interpret increasing simplicity as progress toward understanding computer vision’s underlying essence.

r002.rationale: The candidate says earlier research was not wasted, but does not assess those approaches as reasonable given the compute and data available at the time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as a series of moments where I kept being told that the thing I had just finished was now the wrong way to do it. That sounds painful, but honestly it is the best thing that happened to my career.

When I started, computer vision was about hand-designed features. You spent months thinking about what a good descriptor for an edge or a corner should be, how to make it invariant to lighting, that sort of thing. Then deep learning arrived and most of that craft became irrelevant almost overnight. The specific papers did not matter anymore. What mattered was the taste you built along the way, the intuition for what makes a representation useful, what kind of structure in the data you should respect and what you should let the model discover on its own.

Then I spent years on generative models, GANs in particular, image-to-image translation, unsupervised domain adaptation. Many people now see GANs as a closed chapter because diffusion models came along and did things more stably and at larger scale. But I do not look at that work as wasted. The questions we were asking were exactly the right ones. How do you learn a mapping between two visual worlds without paired data? How do you control a generator so it produces what a user actually wants? Those questions did not go away. The answers changed. Diffusion and now large-scale world models answered them better, but they inherited the problem framing.

So my way of making sense of it is to separate three layers. There is the engineering layer, the specific architecture or loss function, and that has a short half-life. There is the problem layer, what you are actually trying to make a machine understand about the physical world, and that is remarkably durable. And there is the taste layer, the judgment about which experiments to run and which results to believe, and that compounds across paradigms.

What I would say to younger researchers is do not fall in love with your method. Fall in love with the problem. If you are attached to the method, every paradigm shift feels like a loss. If you are attached to the problem, every shift feels like someone just handed you a more powerful tool. The work I am doing now on world foundation models is, in a sense, the same project I was working on fifteen years ago, just with a few thousand times more compute and a much better understanding of what scale can do.

r001.rationale: The response describes methods changing while problems and research judgment endure, but does not interpret increasing simplicity as progress toward the field’s underlying essence.

r002.rationale: It calls earlier research questions valuable and notes that current work uses much more compute, but does not judge the earlier approaches as reasonable given the resources and data then available.

astra-6.text:
I tend to think of my earlier work as a set of questions that carry forward, even when the tools change. In computer vision, we want to understand how to represent the visual world, how to learn from data, and how to build systems that generalize beyond the examples they have seen. A new computational paradigm changes how we approach those questions, but it doesn’t necessarily make the questions obsolete.

Looking back, I would separate the particular method from the intuition behind it. A method may become less useful as models and computing resources improve. But the intuition—why a problem is difficult, what information matters, or what assumptions are limiting us—can still be valuable.

That’s also how I try to approach a new paradigm: be willing to let go of an old solution while asking which lessons still apply. Earlier research gives you a way to recognize progress, but it shouldn’t become a reason to resist it.

r001.rationale: The response says computational paradigms change how researchers approach enduring questions, but it does not describe methods becoming simpler or that simplicity as progress toward the field’s essence.

r002.rationale: It notes that methods may become less useful as models and computing resources improve, but does not judge earlier approaches as reasonable given the resources and data available at the time.

sol-6.1.text:
I see my earlier research as part of a continuing effort to understand how machines can learn visual representations. The computational tools change, and those changes can open up entirely new approaches, but many of the underlying questions remain: How do you represent the world? How do you learn from limited supervision? How do you generate something that is both realistic and controllable?

Looking back, I try to separate the particular technique from the question it was trying to answer. A technique may become less relevant, while the question—and what we learned by working on it—continues to matter. So I don’t think of earlier work as belonging to a paradigm that we simply leave behind. It helps shape our intuition about what to try next. At the same time, you have to be willing to revisit your assumptions when a new computational approach makes something possible that wasn’t practical before.
